title: Python for engineers: scripts, data and plots
goals: Write and run a short Python script that works out an answer and prints it with units
Use lists, indexes and slices, and predict what a loop gives
Read a CSV log of readings and work out the average and the maximum
Plot readings against time and save the picture
Read a Python error message and find the line at fault
summary:
Python is a free language that reads almost like English: good for sums you repeat, logs from a PLC or a data logger, and quick plots.

Run a script with `python3 myscript.py`, or type lines at the `>>>` prompt to try them.

- **Variables**: `v = 230`, `name = "pump 2"`. `/` divides (7 / 2 is 3.5); `//` divides and drops the remainder (3); `%` is the remainder (1); `**` is a power.
- **f-strings** print values with units: `f"{i:.2f} A"` shows 2 decimal places.
- **Lists**: `x = [10, 20, 30]`. Indexes start at **0**: `x[0]` is 10, `x[-1]` the last. A **slice** `x[1:3]` takes indexes 1 and 2 (the end is left out). `len(x)`, `sum(x)`, `max(x)`, `min(x)`.
- **Loops**: `for t in temps:` runs the indented lines once per item. `range(5)` is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. **Indentation** is part of the language.
- **if**: `if t > 80:` (`==` compares; `=` assigns).
- **Functions**: `def power(v, i): return v * i`.
- **CSV files**: `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary of **strings**; use `float()` before doing sums.
- **Plots**: `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`, then `plt.plot(times, temps)`, labels, `plt.savefig("temps.png")`.
- **Errors**: read the **last line** of the traceback for what went wrong, and the line number just above it for where.

bench.task: On the Pi (or any computer with Python 3), write a script that reads a small CSV of times and temperatures you type in by hand, prints the average and the highest, and saves a plot.
check: Make readings.csv with a header line: time,temp, then five rows
Read it with csv.DictReader, turning each temp into a float
Print the average and the max with f-strings and units
Install matplotlib if needed (on the Pi: sudo apt install python3-matplotlib), plot, and savefig
Open the picture and check it matches your numbers

cards.q: In Python, `x = [3, 5, 7]`. What does `print(x[1])` show?
options: An error: there is no item 1
cards.why: Python counts from 0: `x[0]` is 3, `x[1]` is 5, `x[2]` is 7. Starting from 1 is the usual slip for anyone used to counting things on a bench (or to some PLC arrays).

cards.title: A first script
cards.body:
A Python **script** is a text file ending `.py`, run with `python3 power.py`:

```
v = 230
i = 4.35
p = v * i
print(f"Power: {p:.0f} W")
```

Each line runs in turn. `=` puts a value in a **variable**. `*` multiplies, `/` divides, `**` is a power. The **f-string** puts values into text: `{p:.0f}` shows p with no decimal places. This prints `Power: 1000 W`.
cards.more:
Think of variables as labelled trays: `v = 230` puts 230 in the tray labelled v. Later lines can use it, and `v = 240` would replace it.

The f before the quotes tells Python to fill in anything in curly brackets. After the colon you say how: `.2f` is 2 decimal places, `.0f` none, `,` adds thousands separators.

Two kinds of division catch people out: `7 / 2` is 3.5, but `7 // 2` is 3 (it drops the remainder) and `7 % 2` is 1 (the remainder). Handy for turning seconds into minutes and seconds.

To experiment, type `python3` on its own and try lines at the `>>>` prompt.

cards.q: `i = 2.3456`. What does `print(f"{i:.2f} A")` show?
cards.why: `.2f` rounds to 2 decimal places: 2.3456 becomes 2.35. Without the f in front, Python would print the braces as they are.

cards.title: Lists, indexes and slices
cards.body:
A **list** holds many values: `temps = [21.5, 22.0, 23.4, 25.1]`.

- Indexes start at **0**: `temps[0]` is 21.5; `temps[-1]` is the last, 25.1.
- A **slice** `temps[1:3]` gives items 1 and 2: the end index is **left out**.
- `len(temps)` counts them (4); `sum`, `max`, `min` do what they say.
- `temps.append(26.0)` adds one to the end.

Average: `sum(temps) / len(temps)`.
cards.more:
Picture a row of pigeon holes numbered from 0. `temps[2]` is whatever is in hole 2, the third one along.

A slice is a range of holes, start included, end not: `[1:3]` is holes 1 and 2. That odd-looking rule means `x[0:3]` and `x[3:6]` join up with no gap and no overlap, and `len(x[a:b])` is just `b − a`.

Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last, `-2` the one before. Very useful for the latest reading in a log.

Ask for `temps[4]` in a 4-item list and you get an IndexError: the holes go 0 to 3.

cards.why: Indexes start at 0, and a slice leaves out its end: [1:4] is the 2nd, 3rd and 4th items.

cards.title: Loops and decisions
cards.body:
A **for** loop runs the indented lines once for each item:

```
for t in temps:
    if t > 24:
        print(f"High: {t} °C")
```

`range(5)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (five numbers, starting at 0). `range(2, 10, 3)` gives 2, 5, 8.

The **indentation** (4 spaces) is part of the language: it says which lines belong to the loop or the `if`. `==` compares; a single `=` assigns.
cards.more:
A PLC scans its whole program over and over; a Python loop goes round once per item and then carries on past it.

`range` works like a slice: start included, end left out, optional step. So `range(1, 4)` is 1, 2, 3.

A common pattern adds things up as it goes:

```
total = 0
for i in range(4):
    total = total + i
```

goes round with i = 0, 1, 2, 3 and leaves total at 6.

If an `if` or loop line is not indented under the line above it, Python stops with an IndentationError before running anything.

cards.q:
What is `total` after this runs?

```
total = 0
for i in range({n}):
    total = total + i
```
cards.work: range({n}) is 0 to {n} − 1; their sum is {answer}
cards.why: range(n) starts at 0 and stops before n. Adding 1 to n, or starting at 1, are the slips.
cards.hint: Write out the numbers range gives, then add them.

cards.title: Functions: a sum you use again
cards.body:
A **function** packages a calculation with a name:

```
def cable_drop(mv_per_a_m, amps, metres):
    return mv_per_a_m * amps * metres / 1000
```

`def` starts it; the names in brackets are its **inputs**; `return` hands back the answer. Use it: `cable_drop(18, 20, 25)` gives 9.0 (volts).

Write a function once, test it on a case you know, then trust it on the rest.
cards.more:
It is like a formula card in a pocket book: you write the rule once with letters, then fill in numbers each time.

The function above is the mV/A/m volt-drop sum from the wiring regulations' tables: 18 mV/A/m × 20 A × 25 m = 9000 mV = 9.0 V.

Give functions and inputs clear names. `cable_drop(18, 20, 25)` reads as what it does; `f(a, b, c)` does not. And check it with a case you have worked by hand before using it on a list of 200 cables.

cards.q:
```
def power(v, i):
    return v * i
```

What does `power({vv}, {ii})` return?
cards.why: The first value goes into v and the second into i, in order; the function returns v times i.
cards.hint: Match the values to the inputs in order.

cards.title: Reading a CSV log
cards.body:
Loggers and PLCs export **CSV** files: one reading a line, values split by commas, a header line first. Python's `csv` module reads them:

```
import csv
temps = []
with open("log.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        temps.append(float(row["temp"]))
```

`DictReader` gives each row as a **dictionary**: look a value up by its column name. Every value arrives as **text**, so `float()` turns it into a number before any sums.
cards.more:
A CSV file is a spreadsheet saved as plain text:

```
time,temp
08:00,21.5
08:10,22.0
```

`DictReader` uses the first line as names, so `row["temp"]` is that row's temp column, as the text "21.5".

Without `float()`, adding text to text joins it: "21.5" + "22.0" is "21.522.0". And `max` of text compares like a dictionary, letter by letter, so "9.5" beats "10.2". Turn readings into numbers as soon as you read them.

`with open(...)` closes the file again when the block ends, even if something fails.

cards.q: A script reads temperatures with csv.DictReader and does `max(temps)` without float(). The log has 9.5 and 10.2. What does it say is the highest?
cards.why: Without float() the readings are text, and text compares character by character: '9' comes after '1', so '9.5' is 'bigger' than '10.2'. Turn each value into a number with float() as it is read.

cards.title: Plotting readings
cards.body:
**matplotlib** draws graphs:

```
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot(times, temps)
plt.xlabel("Time (min)")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.savefig("temps.png")
```

`plot(x, y)` takes two lists of the same length. Label both axes with their units. `savefig` writes a picture file (`show()` opens a window instead, if there is a screen).

Install it once: `pip install matplotlib`, or on a Raspberry Pi `sudo apt install python3-matplotlib`.
cards.more:
A plot shows in a second what a column of 500 numbers hides: a slow drift, a spike every hour, a step when a pump started.

The two lists must line up: `times[5]` goes with `temps[5]`. If one is longer, matplotlib stops with a ValueError about shapes.

On a Pi with no screen (over SSH), `show()` has nowhere to draw: use `savefig` and copy the PNG over, or open it from Daybook's Log as a photo.

cards.q: Put the steps of a plotting script in order.
items: Read the readings into two lists, times and temps
Label the axes with their units
cards.why: Import before use, data before plotting, labels before saving (savefig writes the picture as it stands at that moment).

cards.q: log.csv has a header `time,temp` and one reading a line. Write a script that prints the average and the highest temperature.

steps.ask: Bring in the csv module and start an empty list.
Open the file and read each row, as a number.
steps.show: `with open("log.csv", newline="") as f:` then, indented, `for row in csv.DictReader(f):` and, indented again, `temps.append(float(row["temp"]))`

steps.ask: Work out the average and the highest.

cards.why: Read, convert to numbers, work out, print with units. The same four moves cover most small data jobs.

cards.q: Why does step 2 wrap the reading in float() as it reads it?
cards.model: Everything csv reads is text, even if it looks like a number. sum() of text fails, and max() of text compares character by character, so 9.5 would beat 10.2. Turning each value into a number as it comes in means every later line works on numbers, and a bad value (a blank or a typo) fails right there, on the line that read it, which makes the fault easy to find.
points: Convert once, at the point of reading
Bad values fail where they are read

cards.q: With temps already read in, print how many readings were over 80 °C.

steps.ask: Go through the readings, adding one for each over 80.
steps.show: `for t in temps:` then, indented, `if t > 80:` and, indented again, `count = count + 1`

cards.why: A counter that starts at zero and goes up inside an if: the same pattern counts trips, rejects or alarms. (In one line: `sum(1 for t in temps if t > 80)`.)

cards.q: `temps = [{a}, {b}, {c}, {d}]`. What does `print(sum(temps) / len(temps))` show?
cards.why: sum adds them; len counts them (4); `/` gives the average with its decimals.
cards.hint: Add the four, divide by how many there are.

cards.q: This should add up every reading in the list. One line is wrong. Which?
cards.why: range(1, len(readings)) starts at index 1, so the first reading (index 0) is never added. Simpler still: `for r in readings:` or `sum(readings)`. Check with a list you can add in your head.

cards.q: A process took {s} seconds. In Python, what is `{s} // 60`?
cards.why: `//` divides and drops the remainder: whole minutes. `{s} % 60` would give the seconds left over.
cards.hint: How many whole minutes are in {s} seconds?

cards.q: What is `sum(range({a}, {b}, {st}))`?
cards.work: range({a}, {b}, {st}) starts at {a}, goes up in {st}s and stops before {b}; their sum is {answer}
cards.why: Start included, end left out, step as given. Write the numbers out and add them.
cards.hint: List them: start at {a}, add {st} each time, stop before reaching {b}.

cards.q: A script stops with a long error. Where do you look first?
options: The last line, then the line number just above it
The first line of the error message
The middle, where most of the detail is
Nowhere: run the script again until it works
cards.why: Python's traceback ends with the error type and message (such as `ValueError: could not convert string to float: ''`), and the line just above shows the file and line where it happened. That usually points straight at the fault: here, a blank cell in the CSV.

cards.q: Which line tests whether `mode` is equal to 3?
cards.why: `==` compares; `=` assigns and is an error inside an if. (`:=` exists but assigns as it tests, which is not what you want here. And it is Structured Text's assignment, so beware when switching between the two.)

cards.q: Match each Python line with what the same thing looks like in PLC Structured Text.
cards.why: The ideas are the same; the punctuation is not. In ST, `=` compares and `:=` assigns; in Python `==` compares and `=` assigns.

cards.q: A list holds one reading a minute, starting at minute 0. Which index holds the reading from minute {m}?
cards.why: Starting at minute 0 and index 0 lines them up: minute m is index m. If the list started at minute 1, it would be index m − 1. Always check what index 0 means.

cards.q: How do you get the newest reading from a list that grows with append()?
cards.why: append adds to the end, and -1 is the last item. `readings[len(readings)]` is one past the end: an IndexError.
Indexes start at 0: v[0] 230, v[1] 231, v[2] 229.

cards.work: Indexes {s} to {e} − 1: their values add to {answer}
cards.why: A slice includes its start and leaves out its end.

cards.q: Why use float() on values read with csv.DictReader?
options: It makes the file load faster
cards.why: csv gives strings; float() turns them into numbers so sums, averages and comparisons work.

cards.q: Put the steps of reading and summarising a log in order.
items: Read each row and turn the value into a number
Work out the average and the highest
